title: Flight-recorder DIMM interposer capturing command history before each error
idea: An aircraft's black box records the minutes before an incident. An FPGA DIMM interposer (two board spins, about $250k) keeps a rolling 1-second ring buffer of ACT/REF commands and temperature. On any corrected or uncorrected ECC event it freezes and dumps the buffer. Deployed on ~200 partner servers within the $1M, it would build the first large dataset linking real flips to real access patterns.
why: Measured distributions of hammer and retention tails, rather than worst-case assumptions, allow right-sized mitigation and refresh margins, possibly a 2x relaxation (facts 3 and 9).

title: NAND-style bad-block maps let partially-good DRAM dies ship
idea: Worse: scrap or down-bin any die whose repair fuses run out. Flip: ship DRAM with a host-visible bad-mat table, like NAND bad blocks, and sell a nominal 32 Gb die as 30 Gb usable, with the OS or CXL controller simply never mapping dead mats.
why: Yield at leading nodes and in HBM (fact 6, 20-30% yield loss): recovering dies that fail on only a few mats can add 10-20% more sellable bits per wafer without new fabs.
note: Partial-good DRAM sales are old; CXL-mapped bad mats is a modern twist.

title: Open-PDK shuttle CMOS plus university BEOL cell post-processing
idea: Combine open-source SKY130/GF180 shuttle chips carrying sense amps, ECC and refresh controllers with university post-processing of capacitor or oxide-TFT arrays on the top-metal pads, giving full-stack reliability testbeds (real arrays plus real ECC) for a few tens of thousands of dollars. Buildable in a university nanofab: low-temperature BEOL steps on diced shuttle die.
why: Speeds iteration on reliability schemes for new cells (facts 2, 3) and builds US memory know-how; a strategy rather than a cell.

title: Parametric charge pumping on common plate regenerates all cells continuously
idea: Effect: parametric amplification via a nonlinear C(V). Each storage node is a nonlinear MOS varactor plus a rectifying junction; a shared AC drive on the common plate pumps charge with a voltage-dependent sign, creating two stable fixed points, so every cell continuously restores itself toward its nearer rail with no row-by-row refresh. Reads compare node charge against a mid-level reference.
why: 10x density: cells tolerating ~1000x more leakage can be 2-terminal crosspoint varactor-diode stacks at 4F^2 in 8 BEOL layers (~10x); refresh counters, timers and restore-heavy sense periphery (fact 7) disappear, holding cost.
note: Parametron-like bistability via plate AC pump; doubts are drive power, crosspoint sneak paths and variability.

title: Federal commons for dead refresh-free memory IP plus shared qualification line
idea: Most refresh-free memory ventures (T-RAM, Z-RAM, Kilopass, Spin Memory and others) died less from physics than from missing reliability data and qualified second sources. Fix: a federal program buys or licenses their patent estates into an open pool and funds a shared U.S. qualification line that runs JEDEC-style retention, endurance, disturb and soft-error testing on every revived cell and publishes the failure-rate data.
why: Cuts years and tens of $M from each zero-refresh technology's path to qualification, lowering capital intensity and lifting U.S. manufacturability.

title: Recompute-as-correction for KV caches and activations
idea: Ideal: memory errors are free to fix because the data can be regenerated. Closest: AI KV-cache and activation buffers are stored in unprotected relaxed-refresh DRAM with only a 16-bit CRC per 1 KB block; on a CRC miss the runtime recomputes that block from upstream tokens or layers instead of correcting it.
why: Facts 3 and 5: removes ECC storage and most refresh for the largest AI memory consumer; recompute costs <0.1% of FLOPs at 1e-7 block error rates.
note: CRC plus regeneration replaces ECC for KV/activations; easy software demo.

title: Eliminate fixed-function reliability: firmware-defined, fleet-learned refresh and ECC subscription
idea: Ship <=400 C BEOL memory modules whose refresh timing, reference levels, ECC codes and remap tables live in updatable controller firmware. The vendor learns drift models from fleet telemetry, pushes updates and sells this as a reliability subscription that raises usable capacity over time.
why: Lets vendors ship early, imperfectly characterized low-thermal-budget memories (as SSD makers do with NAND FTLs) while usable yield keeps improving; faster time-to-market for new memory.

title: Battery cell matching: retention-matched rank assembly
idea: Adapted from EV battery packs, which group cells of matched capacity so one weak cell does not limit the pack: dies are binned by measured retention (e.g., 64/128/256 ms classes) on existing testers, modules are assembled only from same-class dies, and the class is written to SPD so the controller sets tREFI per rank instead of for the worst die in a mixed rank.
why: Refresh cost (fact 3): today one weak die forces worst-case refresh on its whole rank; matched ranks let 60-80% of modules run 2-4x longer refresh, cutting refresh energy and bandwidth loss with only assembly-flow changes.

title: Proof-of-work logic: speculative-decoding drafts run from junk DRAM
idea: Crypto miners shrug off memory errors because every result is cheaply verified. Host LLM speculative-decoding draft models and their caches on retention-reject or relaxed-refresh DIMMs: the full model's verification pass rejects any token a memory error corrupted, so the only cost is a slightly lower acceptance rate.
why: Creates a productive market for weak-bin DRAM (several percent of output) and frees premium HBM for the target model (fact 3).
note: Clever verification-masks-errors insight, but the draft-model memory market is small.

title: SSD-controller playbook: 28nm CXL controller with page-level LDPC
idea: Adapted from NAND flash, which became cheap by pairing weak cells with smart controllers: a 28 nm CXL memory controller built in existing mature logic fabs applies 4 KB-codeword LDPC, with an on-chip SRAM write-combining buffer for read-modify-write, to unmodified commodity or lower-grade DRAM, exposing a byte-addressable device that tolerates raw BER ~1e-4.
why: Supply and cost per bit (facts 3, 4): operators can buy dies that fail JEDEC retention or speed bins at deep discounts and run them at 4-8x longer refresh; costs ~3% parity and ~50-100 ns added latency, acceptable for a CXL tier, with zero new fab capacity.

title: Diversified-portfolio DIMMs mixing vendors inside each codeword
idea: Portfolio theory cuts risk by holding uncorrelated assets. Build ECC modules in which the chips of each codeword come from 2-3 vendors or process lots. Systematic weaknesses (TRR bypass patterns, temperature-dependent retention) then stay uncorrelated, and chipkill absorbs one vendor's failure mode. Module design, qualification and a pilot run fit in $1M.
why: Makes cheaper second-source dies, including new or U.S. entrants, usable at low risk. That diversifies supply and lowers cost per bit.
note: Decorrelates systematic failure modes under chipkill; mixed-vendor timing qualification is the work.

title: Plated-pillar magnetic memory: coincident-current writes, inductive non-destructive reads
idea: Failure mined: plated-wire memory (UNIVAC, Apollo era) read magnetic bits non-destructively with no per-bit transistor but died on hand-assembled wire. Fix: build it monolithically by ALD-coating vertical pillars with a soft magnetic film inside a stack of deposited word planes. Coincident currents in a plane and a pillar write one intersection, and a plane pulse rotates the film so the pillar picks up an inductive or AMR signal without erasing the bit.
why: 10x at the same cost: a transistorless 4F^2 cell per tier and 32 tiers from one hole etch, with unlimited magnetic endurance and no refresh, ~15x bits/mm^2. Periphery scales per plane and per pillar, not per bit.
note: Transistorless 3D magnetic cell with unlimited endurance; doubts: nm-film inductive/AMR signal is tiny, half-select disturb, high write currents.
